topics.title: Biasing a bipolar transistor
topics.summary: Set a steady operating point: a base resistor is simple but depends on β; divider bias with an emitter resistor doesn't.

lensNotes.circuit: Bias sets the transistor's resting point so a signal can swing around it. Divider bias with an emitter resistor sets I_C by voltages and R_E, not by β, which varies widely between parts.

formulas.label: Collector–emitter voltage
formulas.tex: V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_C - I_E R_E\ \ (\text{no } R_E\text{: } V_{CC} - I_C R_C)

prerequisiteNotes.bjt_intro: Biasing uses I_C = β·I_B and V_BE ≈ 0.7 V to put the transistor at a chosen operating point.
prerequisiteNotes.dividers: The standard bias network is a voltage divider on the base, stiff enough that the base current barely loads it.

goals: Find the operating point (I_C and V_CE) of a stage biased by a single base resistor, or by a divider with an emitter resistor
Check that a bias divider is stiff (its current at least ten times the base current) and that V_CE leaves the transistor well inside the active region
Explain why an emitter resistor makes the collector current nearly independent of β, while a single base resistor makes it proportional to β
Predict how the operating point moves when the transistor is swapped for one with a different β, or when it warms up
topics.intuition: With a stiff divider holding the base voltage and a resistor R_E in the emitter, the emitter sits one V_BE (about 0.7 V) below the base, so in the active region R_E sets the collector current, I_C ≈ (V_B − 0.7 V)/R_E, and β hardly matters.
topics.why: Biasing sets the operating point (Q-point): the resting collector current and voltage a signal will swing around. A single base resistor fixes I_B, so I_C = β·I_B follows β, which differs two or three times between parts and rises with temperature. A divider fixes the base voltage instead. V_BE barely changes, so V_E = V_B − V_BE is fixed, and so is I_E = V_E/R_E. If I_C tries to rise, the drop across R_E rises, V_BE shrinks, and the base current falls back: negative feedback. β decides only how much base current flows, and a stiff divider supplies it without sagging much.
topics.explanation: A transistor amplifies only while it is in its active region, so a circuit must first set its resting state: a steady collector current and collector–emitter voltage, called the operating point. The simplest bias is one resistor R_B from the supply to the base. It fixes I_B = (V_CC − 0.7 V)/R_B, and I_C = β·I_B. But β differs two or three times between transistors of the same type, so a part with twice the β runs at twice the current, perhaps into saturation. Divider bias fixes the base voltage instead: R1 from the supply and R2 to ground give V_B = V_CC·R2/(R1 + R2). The emitter sits one V_BE lower, V_E = V_B − 0.7 V, and a resistor R_E turns that into a current: I_E = V_E/R_E, with I_C ≈ I_E. β has dropped out. This is accurate when the base current barely loads the divider; the usual rule of thumb is a divider current at least ten times I_B at the lowest β (a stiff divider). Otherwise, use the divider's Thevenin equivalent. Finally, find V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C − V_E and check that it is well above 0.2 V, so the transistor really is active.

workedExample.problem: A 12 V stage uses divider bias: R1 = 47 kΩ from the supply to the base, R2 = 10 kΩ from the base to ground, R_E = 1.0 kΩ in the emitter, and R_C = 3.9 kΩ in the collector. The transistor is a small-signal NPN such as a 2N3904; assume β = 100 and V_BE = 0.7 V. Find I_C and V_CE, and check that the divider is stiff. Then see what a β = 300 part does, here and in the same stage biased by a single base resistor, and what warming the transistor by 50 °C does.
steps: Base voltage (stiff-divider model: base current ignored): V_B = 12 V × 10 kΩ / (47 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 2.105 V.

Collector: R_C drops 1.405 mA × 3.9 kΩ = 5.481 V, so V_C = 12 V − 5.481 V = 6.519 V and V_CE = 6.519 V − 1.405 V = 5.11 V. That is far above 0.2 V: the transistor is in the active region, as the model assumed.

Stiffness: the divider carries 12 V / (47 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 0.211 mA. The base needs I_B = I_E/(β + 1) = 1.405 mA / 101 = 13.9 µA, so the divider current is 15 times I_B: stiff. The stiff model ignores the base current's pull on V_B. Counting it (the divider looks like 2.105 V behind R1∥R2 = 8.25 kΩ): I_E = 1.405 V / (1.0 kΩ + 8.25 kΩ/101) = 1.30 mA, 7.5% lower. A β = 300 part draws less base current and gets 1.37 mA.
A β = 300 part: nothing in the first three steps contains β, so I_C stays at about 1.405 mA and V_CE at about 5.11 V. The new part draws only a third of the base current, 1.405 mA / 301 = 4.67 µA.

For comparison, bias the same transistor with a single base resistor (R_E removed, emitter grounded, same R_C). For about 1.4 mA at β = 100, it needs I_B = 14 µA, so R_B = (12 V − 0.7 V) / 14 µA ≈ 810 kΩ; use 820 kΩ (E12). Then I_B = 11.3 V / 820 kΩ = 13.78 µA, I_C = 100 × 13.78 µA = 1.378 mA, and V_CE = 12 V − 1.378 mA × 3.9 kΩ = 6.63 V.

Swap in the β = 300 part: the active-region model asks for I_C = 300 × 13.78 µA = 4.13 mA, which would need 4.13 mA × 3.9 kΩ = 16.1 V across R_C, more than the 12 V supply. The transistor saturates instead, at I_C = (12 V − 0.2 V) / 3.9 kΩ = 3.03 mA with V_CE ≈ 0.2 V: it can no longer amplify.

Temperature, divider bias (−2 mV/°C at a fixed current): At 50 °C warmer, V_BE ≈ 0.7 V − 2 mV/°C × 50 °C = 0.6 V, so V_E = 2.105 V − 0.6 V = 1.505 V and I_C ≈ 1.505 mA, 7% more; V_CE falls to 12 V − 1.505 mA × 3.9 kΩ − 1.505 V = 4.63 V, still active. The 0.1 V shift is 7% of V_E; a larger V_E would make the drift a smaller fraction.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 4 "Bipolar Junction Transistors", section "Biasing calculations", subsection "Base Bias"
sources.note: With one resistor from the supply to the base, KVL with V_BE ≈ 0.7 V sets the base current, so the emitter current follows β, roughly tripling when a β = 100 part is swapped for β = 300, and the bias is not temperature stable.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 4 "Bipolar Junction Transistors", section "Biasing calculations", subsection "Emitter-bias"
sources.note: An emitter resistor gives negative feedback: a rise in emitter current raises its drop, which reduces the base drive and pulls the current back, so the bias depends much less on β, temperature, and tolerances.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Transistor biasing" (last update 27 September 2025), ch. 2 "Tutorial", section 2.4 "Biasing networks"
sources.note: A divider R1/R2 sets the base bias at V_CC·R2/(R1 + R2); the base current sags it slightly, mostly through R_E seen as about (β + 1)·R_E from the base, which is usually much larger than R2, so the simple divider formula holds.

templates.prompt: An NPN transistor (β = {beta}) has its base fed from {Vcc} through R_B = {Rb}, and its emitter grounded. What is the collector current (assume the active region)?
templates.explanation: I_B = (V_CC − 0.7) / R_B = ({Vcc} − 0.7) / {Rb} = {Ib}. Then I_C = β I_B = {beta} × {Ib} = {answer}. Because this depends directly on β, which varies a lot between parts, it's a fragile bias method.
hints: Find the base current first: R_B has V_CC − V_BE across it.

misconceptions.feedback: The base sits 0.7 V above ground, so R_B has V_CC − 0.7 across it.
That's the base current. Multiply by β for the collector current.

followUps.prompt: In this circuit, what sets the collector current?

choices.text: R_B fixes the base current, and the transistor multiplies it by its own β, so a different part gives a different I_C
choices.feedback: Right: nothing in the circuit pushes back if β is different.

choices.text: R_C, by Ohm's law
choices.feedback: In the active region, R_C doesn't set the current; it only takes whatever drop β·I_B·R_C produces. R_C limits the current only once the transistor saturates.

choices.text: The supply voltage divided by R_B
choices.feedback: That (less 0.7 V) is the base current, not the collector current; the transistor then multiplies it by β.

choices.text: The 0.7 V base–emitter drop
choices.feedback: V_BE is almost fixed and only trims the voltage across R_B; it doesn't set the ratio of the currents.

followUps.explanation: Here I_B = (V_CC − 0.7 V)/R_B is set by the resistor alone, and I_C = β·I_B (Bipolar transistor basics). The circuit has no way to notice or correct the collector current, so a part with twice the β runs at twice the current, perhaps into saturation. Divider bias with an emitter resistor fixes exactly this.

templates.prompt: A transistor with its emitter grounded carries I_C = {Ic} through a collector resistor R_C = {Rc} from {Vcc}. What is V_CE?
templates.explanation: R_C drops I_C·R_C = {Ic} × {Rc} = {VRc}. The rest of the supply is across the transistor: V_CE = {Vcc} − {VRc} = {answer}. That is well above the 0.2 V or so of saturation, so the transistor is in the active region, as the given I_C assumes.
hints: KVL from V_CC through R_C and the transistor to ground.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the drop across R_C. V_CE is what's left: V_CC − I_C R_C.

templates.formulaStepsWhy: One relation: the collector loop, V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C.

templates.prompt: A transistor is biased by a stiff divider from {Vcc}: R1 = {R1} (to Vcc) and R2 = {R2} (to ground), with R_E = {Re} in the emitter and R_C = 1 kΩ in the collector. Estimate the collector current (I_C ≈ I_E).
templates.explanation: A stiff divider sets V_B = {Vcc} × {R2} / ({R1} + {R2}) = {Vb}. The emitter is one drop lower, V_E = {Ve}, so I_E = V_E / R_E = {Ve} / {Re} = {answer} ≈ I_C. β doesn't appear, which is why this bias is stable. Check the region: V_CE = {Vcc} − I_C × 1 kΩ − V_E = {Vce}, well above 0.2 V, so the transistor is active and the model holds.
hints: Find the base voltage from the divider, then the emitter voltage.

misconceptions.feedback: The emitter is 0.7 V below the base; subtract V_BE before dividing by R_E.

steps: A stiff divider sets the base: V_B = {Vcc} × {R2}/({R1} + {R2}) = {Vb}.
The emitter sits one diode drop lower: V_E = V_B − 0.7 V = {Ve}.
The emitter current is V_E/R_E, and I_C ≈ I_E: {Ve}/{Re} = {answer}.

followUps.prompt: The answer doesn't contain β. Why does R_E hold the collector current so steady?

choices.text: If I_C tried to rise, the drop across R_E would rise too, leaving less of the fixed base voltage across the base–emitter junction; that reduces V_BE and so reduces the base current: negative feedback
choices.feedback: Right: the emitter voltage is fed back against the fixed base voltage.

choices.text: R_E limits the current like a fuse
choices.feedback: A fuse acts only on a fault, by breaking the circuit. R_E acts all the time, by raising the emitter voltage whenever the current rises.

choices.text: R_E makes every transistor's β the same
choices.feedback: β still varies from part to part; R_E makes the collector current insensitive to it.

choices.text: The divider supplies the collector current, so β can't affect it
choices.feedback: The collector current comes from the supply through R_C. The divider only fixes the base voltage.

followUps.explanation: The divider fixes V_B (Voltage and current dividers). The emitter must sit one diode drop below it, so V_E, and therefore I_E = V_E/R_E, is fixed too. Anything that tries to raise I_C (a higher-β part, or a warmer transistor) raises V_E, which reduces V_BE and so reduces the base current: negative feedback. β decides only how much base current is needed, and a stiff divider supplies that without its voltage moving much.

templates.prompt: Why is voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor preferred over a single base resistor?

choices.text: The collector current hardly depends on β, which varies widely between transistors and with temperature
choices.feedback: Yes: I_C ≈ (V_B − 0.7)/R_E, and β drops out.

choices.text: It gives more voltage gain
choices.feedback: An unbypassed R_E actually lowers the gain; its job is stability.

choices.text: It uses fewer components
choices.feedback: It uses more (two divider resistors plus R_E).

choices.text: It removes the 0.7 V base–emitter drop
choices.feedback: V_BE is still there. Its drift (about −2 mV/°C) moves V_E, so designers make V_E a volt or more, where that drift is a small fraction.

templates.explanation: With a single base resistor, I_C = β I_B follows β directly. With divider bias, R_E sets I_C ≈ (V_B − 0.7)/R_E, independent of β. The emitter resistor's negative feedback also counters temperature drift.
templates.noDrawing: compares two bias schemes in general; no single circuit or values

templates.prompt: Why is a bias circuit whose collector current depends directly on β considered fragile?

choices.text: β varies widely between parts and with temperature, so I_C would too
choices.feedback: Right: β can vary 2–3× between transistors of the same type. Divider bias with an emitter resistor makes I_C depend on resistors instead.

choices.text: β is always exactly 100, so it doesn't matter
choices.feedback: Datasheets give a wide range, like 100–300, and it shifts with temperature and current.

choices.text: β only matters for PNP transistors
choices.feedback: The β spread affects NPN and PNP alike.

choices.text: β changes the supply voltage
choices.feedback: β affects currents, not the supply.

templates.explanation: Base-resistor bias gives I_C = β·I_B, so a transistor with twice the β runs at twice the current, perhaps into saturation. A stiff divider plus R_E sets V_E and so I_E ≈ V_E/R_E, almost independent of β.
hints: Look up how much β varies on a typical datasheet.
templates.noDrawing: a general question about β spread; no particular circuit is described

templates.prompt: Two boards are built from the same parts list: a 12 V supply, R_B = 680 kΩ from the supply to the base, R_C = 2.7 kΩ from the supply to the collector, the emitter grounded, and an NPN transistor of one type whose datasheet gives β from 100 to 300 at this current. Every resistor measures within 5% of its marked value, and both bases read about 0.7 V. On board A the collector reads 7 V; on board B it reads 0.2 V. What is the most likely cause of the difference?

choices.text: Board B's transistor has a higher β, so with the same I_B, β·I_B asks for more than R_C can pass
choices.feedback: Right: R_B fixes I_B the same on both boards, so I_C = β·I_B follows each part's β, and nothing in the circuit pulls it back.

choices.text: Board B's transistor has a lower β, so it can't hold its collector up and the collector sinks to 0.2 V
choices.feedback: A lower β means less collector current, so R_C drops less and the collector sits higher, toward 12 V. A collector pulled down to 0.2 V means R_C is carrying more current, not less.

choices.text: Board B's base–emitter junction drops 0.6 V instead of 0.7 V, so its base current is much larger
choices.feedback: R_B would then have 11.4 V across it instead of 11.3 V: under 1% more base current. Board B carries more than twice board A's collector current, which a 0.1 V shift in V_BE can't explain.

choices.text: Board A's transistor is faulty, because a working one in this circuit sits fully on, with V_CE about 0.2 V
choices.feedback: Board A is in the active region, which is what this bias is for: I_C = (12 V − 7 V)/2.7 kΩ = 1.85 mA from about 17 µA of base current, a β near 111, inside the datasheet's range. Board B is the one that has left the active region.

templates.explanation: Both boards have the same base current: I_B = (12 V − 0.7 V)/680 kΩ = 16.6 µA, set by R_B alone. Board A: R_C drops 12 V − 7 V = 5 V, so I_C = 5 V/2.7 kΩ = 1.85 mA and β = 1.85 mA/16.6 µA ≈ 111. Board B: R_C can pass at most (12 V − 0.2 V)/2.7 kΩ = 4.37 mA, and a part saturates once β·I_B reaches that, at β = 4.37 mA/16.6 µA ≈ 263, still inside the 100–300 spread. Base-resistor bias passes the β spread straight into I_C, so the same parts list gives one board in the active region and another saturated. Divider bias with an emitter resistor sets I_C from V_E/R_E instead.
hints: What sets the base current, and does it depend on the transistor?
I_C = β·I_B until R_C runs out of voltage at (V_CC − 0.2 V)/R_C.

followUps.prompt: Which change to the circuit would make both boards run at nearly the same collector current?

choices.text: Bias the base from a stiff divider and add an emitter resistor, so V_E/R_E sets I_C
choices.feedback: Right: V_B is fixed by the divider, V_E sits one V_BE below it, and I_E = V_E/R_E contains no β.

choices.text: Use a smaller R_C on both boards, so board B's collector has room to stay out of saturation
choices.feedback: That could keep board B out of saturation, but I_C = β·I_B still follows β: board B would still run at about 2.4 times board A's current or more.

choices.text: Use a larger R_B on both boards, so board B's higher β has less base current to multiply
choices.feedback: That lowers both base currents by the same factor, so both collector currents fall, but their ratio is still β_B/β_A.

choices.text: Fit a higher-voltage supply to both boards, so board B's collector has more room above 0.2 V
choices.feedback: More supply raises I_B on both boards in the same proportion; the collector currents still differ by the ratio of the two βs.

followUps.explanation: Any bias that fixes I_B leaves I_C = β·I_B, so the part-to-part β spread goes straight into I_C. A stiff divider fixes V_B instead, and the emitter resistor turns V_E = V_B − 0.7 V into I_E = V_E/R_E. β then decides only how much base current the divider must supply.

templates.prompt: An NPN transistor is biased by a single base resistor R_B = {Rb} from {Vcc}, with R_C = {Rc} in the collector and the emitter grounded. It runs in the active region. The transistor (β = {beta}) is replaced by another of the same type with β = {new_beta}, within the datasheet's spread. What happens to the collector current?

whatIf.factorHint: R_B fixes I_B = (V_CC − 0.7 V)/R_B whatever the transistor, so the new part sees the same base current. Look at how β enters I_C = β·I_B.

feedback.down: A higher β never chokes the collector: R_B still sets the base current at (V_CC − 0.7 V)/R_B whatever the transistor, and I_C is that base current times the part's own β.
feedback.same: Nothing holds I_C steady here: R_B fixes the base current whatever the transistor, and the transistor multiplies that same base current by its own β. Nothing in the circuit feeds back to pull I_B down when β is high.

templates.explanation: The base current I_B = ({Vcc} − 0.7 V)/{Rb} = {Ib} is set by R_B alone and doesn't depend on the transistor, so I_C = β·I_B follows β: {before} → {after}. The stage stays in the active region (V_CE is still {VceAfter}), but its operating point has moved a long way, and a wider β spread could push it into saturation. With divider bias and an emitter resistor, β drops out instead.
hints: Does the new transistor change the base current?

templates.prompt: A transistor stage runs from {Vcc} with a divider on its base (R1 = {R1} to the supply, R2 = {R2} to ground), R_E = {Re} in the emitter, and R_C = {Rc} in the collector. The divider is stiff: its current is more than ten times the base current, so treat V_B as the unloaded divider voltage. The transistor (β = {beta}) is replaced by one with β = {new_beta}. What happens to the collector current, to within 5%?

feedback.up: A single base resistor would double it (I_C = β·I_B). Here V_B, V_E, and R_E set I_E, and none of them depends on β. The only effect is the smaller base-current drop in R1∥R2, a rise of under 5% (see the explanation).
feedback.down: A higher β never lowers the current by itself, and V_B, V_E, and R_E, which set the current here, haven't changed.

templates.explanation: The divider fixes V_B = {Vb} (Voltage and current dividers), the emitter sits at V_E = V_B − 0.7 V = {Ve}, and R_E turns that into I_E = {Ve}/{Re} = {before} ≈ I_C. β isn't in that chain, so in the stiff-divider model the current stays at {after}; the higher-β part draws only half the base current. Treating the divider as a Thevenin source (R_th = R1∥R2 = {Rth}) shows the small leftover effect: counting the base current's drop across R_th, I_C really moves from about {IcTh} to {IcTh2}, under 5%, where a single base resistor would double it. This is R_E's negative feedback at work.
hints: Which of V_B, V_E, and R_E depends on β?

templates.prompt: A transistor stage runs from 12 V. A divider sets its base: R1 = {R1} to the supply and R2 = 10 kΩ to ground. Assume β is high enough that the base current doesn't load the divider, so treat V_B as the unloaded divider voltage. R_C = 2.2 kΩ is in the collector. Choose the emitter resistor R_E (an E24 value) so the collector current is {Ic}, within 8% (take V_BE = 0.7 V and I_C ≈ I_E).
templates.explanation: The divider sets V_B = 12 V × 10 kΩ/({R1} + 10 kΩ) = {Vb} (Voltage and current dividers). The emitter sits one V_BE lower, V_E = {Ve}, and that voltage is across R_E, so I_E = V_E/R_E. For I_C ≈ I_E = {Ic}: R_E = {Ve}/{Ic} = {Rex}; pick the nearest E24 value. β doesn't enter, which is the point of this bias. R_C doesn't either: it only sets V_CE = 12 V − I_C·R_C − V_E = {Vce}, which keeps the transistor well out of saturation.
hints: What voltage does the divider put on the base, and where does that leave the emitter?

followUps.prompt: R_C = 2.2 kΩ didn't appear anywhere in your calculation of I_C. Why not?

choices.text: In the active region, the collector passes whatever current the base–emitter loop sets; R_C only decides how far the collector voltage falls
choices.feedback: Right: V_B, V_BE, and R_E fix I_E, and the collector collects nearly all of it. R_C turns that current into a voltage drop.

choices.text: It does matter: a larger R_C would cut the current, by Ohm's law
choices.feedback: Only once R_C is so large that the collector falls to about 0.2 V and the transistor saturates. Until then, a larger R_C only lowers the collector voltage; I_C stays at V_E/R_E.

choices.text: The collector current doesn't flow through R_C
choices.feedback: It does: it comes from the supply through R_C into the collector. R_C carries it but doesn't set its size.

choices.text: R_C is small next to R1, so it can be neglected
choices.feedback: Size isn't the reason: R_C is in a different loop from the divider. Even a much larger R_C leaves I_C unchanged as long as the transistor stays out of saturation.

followUps.explanation: The loop that sets the current is the divider, the base–emitter junction, and R_E: V_E = V_B − 0.7 V, so I_E = V_E/R_E. The reverse-biased collector junction collects almost all of I_E whatever its voltage, so the collector behaves like a current source. R_C is on the other side of that current source: it sets V_C = 12 V − I_C·R_C, which is how a later amplifier turns a current change into a voltage change.

templates.prompt: This stage runs from 12 V with divider bias: R1 = {R1} and R2 = {R2} set the base, R_E = {Re} is in the emitter, and R_C = {Rc} in the collector (the transistor's β is about 150). When the circuit is healthy, a voltmeter with its black lead on ground reads {h0} at the base, {h1} at the emitter, and {h2} at the collector. The readings are below. Which fault explains them?

faults.feedback: With R1 open, nothing would feed the base from the supply: R2 would pull it to 0 V, the transistor would be cut off, the emitter would read 0 V, and the collector the full 12 V.
faults.why: The base and emitter read 0 V and the collector 12 V: the transistor is cut off because its base has been pulled to ground. R2 can do that only if nothing feeds the base from the supply, so R1 is open.

faults.feedback: With R2 open, R1 alone would feed the base, with nothing to hold it down at the divider voltage. The base would rise to several volts, the emitter would follow about 0.7 V below it, and the transistor would saturate, with the collector only about 0.1 V above the emitter.
faults.why: The base and emitter have both risen far above normal, still about 0.7 V apart, and the collector has fallen to just above the emitter: the transistor is saturated. The base is getting far more bias than the divider gives, which happens when R1 alone drives it with nothing from the base to ground. R2 is open.

faults.feedback: With R_E open, the emitter current would have no path: the collector would sit at 12 V with no current, the base would rise slightly, to the unloaded divider voltage, and the emitter, held only by the meter's 10 MΩ, would read only about 0.4 V below the base.
faults.why: The collector reads 12 V, so no collector current flows, yet the base sits at its divider voltage (slightly above normal, {Vb} unloaded) and the emitter follows it: the transistor is biased on, but its current has nowhere to leave. The emitter reads less than 0.7 V below the base because its only path is the voltmeter's 10 MΩ, which draws a fraction of a microamp, and at so small a current V_BE is only about 0.4 V (about 60 mV less for every tenfold drop in current). R_E is open.

faults.feedback: With R_C open, the collector could draw nothing from the supply, so the emitter current would all have to come in through the base, from the divider. The base would sag below 1 V, the emitter would read only one or two tenths of a volt, and the collector would read close to the emitter.
faults.why: The base has sagged well below its divider voltage, and the emitter reads only one or two tenths of a volt, so far less current than normal flows in R_E. The collector reads close to the emitter, as if saturated, yet hardly any current flows: the collector has lost its supply. With R_C open, the whole emitter current must come in through the base, from the divider, which can supply only a fraction of a milliamp, so the base is pulled down. The collector reads only a few tens of millivolts above the emitter: with no collector current, both junctions are forward biased, and a saturated transistor carrying no collector current has almost no voltage from collector to emitter. The meter's 10 MΩ draws only nanoamps from it.

The current in R_C and R_E isn't controlled by the base at all; it flows straight through a collector–emitter short. Check: 12 V × {Re}/({Rc} + {Re}) = {Vshort}.

R_E sets the current only through the voltage across it, I_E = V_E/R_E. With R_E bridged, the base–emitter junction clamps the base at one V_BE and draws all the current the divider can give, about ({Vb} − 0.7 V)/(R1 ∥ R2) = {Ibr}. β times that, about {Ibeta}, is far more than the {Isat} R_C can pass.

templates.explanation: Start with the emitter. In the active region it sits one V_BE, about 0.7 V, below the base, and V_E/R_E is the current it carries. Then place the collector: well between the emitter and 12 V means the transistor is active; at 12 V means no collector current; within a few tenths of a volt of the emitter means saturation, unless almost no current flows (the emitter voltage tells which). A base pulled to 0 V with everything off: the base has lost its feed. Base and emitter both high with the collector just above the emitter: too much bias, saturated. Emitter at 0 V with the base clamped at 0.7 V: nothing in the emitter limits the current. Base at its divider voltage, collector at 12 V: the current has no way out. Collector equal to emitter, both above the base: the transistor is shorted, collector to emitter.
